screens.title: Documenting Software Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why documenting software architecture is an essential engineering practice and how to make documentation clear, concise, and maintainable. Good architecture documentation is primarily a communication tool: it preserves the big decisions, explains the rationale, and helps teams make consistent choices as the system evolves. Poor or missing documentation creates confusion, causes repeated debates, and adds risk when people assume the reasons behind past choices. We will explore common architectural views, practical notation approaches like UML and the C4 model, and a lightweight way to record decisions using Architecture Decision Records. Throughout, the emphasis is on recording the why and the what at the right level of abstraction — not the implementation details that rapidly go out of date. You will see concrete examples and a short ADR template you can reuse. By the end you'll be able to pick the right view for your audience, create a C4-style container diagram for a small system, and write an ADR so future team members can understand why a choice was made. Think about one decision in your current project that would be clearer with an ADR.

screens.title: Why document architecture?
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural documentation exists to communicate intent and constraints, not to replicate code or become a long, unmaintainable manual. Think of documentation as a shared vocabulary: it tells future maintainers what mattered when key choices were made and why certain trade-offs were accepted. For example, an ADR that explains choosing a particular database clarifies performance, consistency, and operational expectations; without that record, new engineers may propose incompatible changes that reintroduce problems. A common misconception is that more detail is always better. In practice, overly detailed architecture documents that mirror code become obsolete and create extra upkeep. Instead, aim for just enough information to answer stakeholder questions: the what, the why, and the consequences. Use short diagrams to show structure and brief ADRs to capture decisions. Another pitfall is keeping documentation isolated from the team’s workflow. Store diagrams and ADRs alongside code or in the team’s primary documentation site so they are discoverable and versioned. Takeaway: document the rationale and the structural overview; avoid implementation detail. A reflective question: which recent change in your project would have been faster if an ADR had existed?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Documentation should convey architectural intent, rationale, and consequences without duplicating implementation detail.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Why document architecture?

Documentation as communication

Document the why and the what. Avoid excessive implementation detail that quickly becomes outdated.

Why it helps
Prevents repeated debates, aids onboarding, and supports consistent implementation.
Common mistake
Too much detail that mirrors code results in brittle, obsolete docs.
Key Takeaway

Keep architecture documents concise, focused on intent, rationale, and consequences; make them discoverable and versioned.

Concrete example
An ADR that records choosing PostgreSQL for strong transactional guarantees explains why eventual consistency was avoided for order processing. With that ADR, developers know that changing to a schema-less store requires re-evaluating transactional expectations and adding compensating mechanisms.
Misconception check: Documentation does not need to include code-level migrations or function bodies. Those belong in code and release notes. The architecture artifact should guide those implementations without duplicating them.
Try this
Write a one-paragraph ADR for a recent architecture choice you can justify in two sentences.

screens.title: Good documentation practices
screens.narratorSegment: Creating useful architecture documentation is a process that balances clarity, discoverability, and maintenance. Start by deciding the audience for each artifact: developers need a logical view and components; operations need deployment and process views. Next, choose the notation and level of detail: use UML where precise structural or behavioral detail is required, and prefer C4 diagrams for layered, audience-friendly descriptions. Third, place artifacts where teams already work — version control, developer portals, or the primary docs site — and link them to code and tickets. A common mistake is producing documents that live in a separate, rarely-visited wiki. Finally, set an update process: lightweight ADRs updated when decisions change, and diagrams reviewed during architecture reviews or major releases. For example, when a team migrates to containerized deployments, update the deployment view and record the decision in an ADR. This process reduces drift and keeps documentation actionable. Checkpoint: after documenting, ask whether the artifact answers a practitioner’s top three questions; if not, pare it back or reframe it for the intended role. Good documentation practices means document with a clear audience, store artifacts where teams work, and update them as part of the development lifecycle.. In practical terms, concise, discoverable, and role-focused documentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Documentation process steps
1
Identify the audience
Tailor the view and level of detail to stakeholders' questions.

Choose notation

Concrete scenario
A team adopting containers updated the deployment view to show new clusters, and created an ADR to record reasons for instance sizing. Operations used the updated deployment view to adjust monitoring and capacity planning, avoiding misconfiguration during the rollout.

screens.title: Architectural Views — Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural views let you present the system from perspectives that match stakeholder concerns. The Logical View explains functional decomposition: major components, responsibilities, and interfaces — valuable for developers planning feature work. The Process View shows runtime behavior: concurrency, message flows, and sequence of operations — operations and performance engineers rely on it. The Deployment View maps components to physical or virtual infrastructure — critical for deployment, scaling, and network configuration. The Physical View, when separate, focuses on hardware and network topology. Finally, the Development View organizes modules and libraries to show how the codebase is managed and built. Each view answers a distinct set of questions: Who implements which responsibility? How do runtime parts communicate? Where do components run? When you prepare documentation, choose the view that answers the most urgent question for your audience. For example, when addressing latency problems, the Process View and Deployment View will be most useful together. A common misconception is to create a single monolithic diagram; instead create multiple concise views and link them to the relevant ADRs or artifacts so reviewers can navigate from rationale to structure.

keyIdea.text: Different views answer different stakeholder questions — pick the view that matches the problem you need to solve.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Architectural Views — Overview
Views and their purpose
Logical View: Functional decomposition and component responsibilities.
Process View: Runtime behavior, concurrency and message flows.
Deployment View: Mapping of components to infrastructure, containers, and network.
Development View: Module structure, libraries, and build boundaries.
Example: latency investigation
When investigating latency, start with the Process View to see message sequencing, then inspect the Deployment View to find network hops and resource placement. Developers may then consult the Logical View for algorithmic hotspots. Linking these views with ADRs that recorded past scaling decisions helps interpret trade-offs.
Checklist
  • - Create focused diagrams per stakeholder.
  • - Keep diagrams short; use links to deeper context.
  • - Store artifacts in version control with ADRs.

screens.title: Logical View in detail
screens.narratorSegment: The Logical View describes the system’s structure in terms of responsibilities and interactions. It groups related functionality into components, and it shows interfaces and relationships between those components. This view helps developers understand where features live and how modules collaborate. A concrete example: an e-commerce domain might include components such as Catalog, Cart, Order, and Payment. The Logical View shows the responsibilities of each component and the interfaces they expose, helping developers avoid coupling unrelated concerns. One common misconception is treating the Logical View as an implementation blueprint — it should remain at a higher level than classes or method signatures. If you need class-level detail, keep it in separate artifacts or auto-generated diagrams. For practical use, annotate each component with a short responsibility line and link to the ADRs that influenced its design. That way, developers can read the rationale for why a component exists or why certain responsibilities were separated. Closing question: which component in your application has unclear responsibilities and would benefit from a concise logical diagram? Logical View in detail means shows functional components and responsibilities to guide implementation without prescribing code.. In practical terms, functional decomposition, components, and responsibilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Logical View
What it shows
Components, responsibilities, and interfaces. Use short labels and avoid code detail.
Catalog
Responsibilities: product metadata, search index.
Order
Responsibilities: order lifecycle, validation.
Concrete analogy
Think of the Logical View as a departmental chart for a company: it shows who is responsible for which business function, without listing each employee’s task. Developers use it to find where to add a feature and to avoid crossing responsibilities.
Misconception
Avoid treating the Logical View as a class diagram. Keep it stable and high-level; link to code-level artifacts when needed.

screens.title: Process View in detail
screens.narratorSegment: The Process View describes how parts of the system behave at runtime: which processes exist, how they communicate, and where concurrency or synchronization matters. This view is essential when reasoning about performance, reliability, and failure modes. A practical example is a photo-upload pipeline: a front-end process receives an upload, an A P I process stores metadata, and a background worker resizes images and writes to object storage. The Process View shows those interactions and the sequence of messages. It also highlights concurrency points where queuing or locking may be used. A typical misconception is believing the Process View must show every low-level thread or actor; instead show the logical runtime participants, the message paths, and where contention or scalability concerns arise. Use sequence or activity-style diagrams for clarity. When you pair the Process View with a Deployment View, you can reason about latency caused by network hops or co-location. Final check: ask whether the Process View reveals likely bottlenecks and failure modes for the scenario you are analyzing. Process View in detail means shows runtime participants and message flows to reason about concurrency and performance.. In practical terms, runtime behavior, concurrency, and message flows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Process View
Process example: photo upload pipeline
Front-end process → API process → background worker → object storage. Indicate queues, retries, and parallel workers where appropriate. Highlight where latency or contention may appear.
Concurrency hotspot
Image resizing worker pool and queue length.
Failure mode
What happens if the storage service is slow or unavailable.
Misconception
Don't overload the Process View with thread-level details. Show logical processes and their communication patterns.
When to use

Use the Process View when troubleshooting performance or designing resilience strategies like retries and backoff.

screens.title: Deployment and Physical Views
screens.narratorSegment: The Deployment View maps software components to hardware or virtual infrastructure and explains network topology, co-location, and resource boundaries. This view answers questions operations teams care about: where do services run, what network connections are required, and how do data stores align with compute? For example, a microservice may run in a container orchestrated by a cluster, with a managed database hosted separately. The Deployment View would show the cluster, the database instances, load balancers, and any external services. A key practical benefit is enabling capacity planning and identifying single points of failure. A common error is including internal component responsibilities in the Deployment View; keep the view focused on runtime placement. Pair the Deployment View with ADRs that record choices like instance types or managed service trade-offs so future teams understand the operational reasoning. Closing thought: when you change deployment architecture, update the Deployment View and create an ADR to record the operational impacts and alternatives considered. Deployment and Physical Views means shows how components map to physical or virtual infrastructure to guide operations and capacity planning.. In practical terms, mapping software to infrastructure and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Deployment and Physical Views
What to include
Nodes, containers, cloud instances, load balancers, storage services, and network connections. Indicate co-location and resilience measures like autoscaling and failover groups.
Operations benefit
Deployers can plan capacity and understand fault domains.
Record choices
Link ADRs for instance sizing and managed services.
Concrete scenario
When moving to a managed database, document the network rules, backup schedules, and expected throughput. An ADR should explain trade-offs, operational constraints, and rollback paths.
Misconception
Don’t mix deployment topology with logical responsibilities; keep them separate artifacts linked by references.

screens.title: Development View and maintainability
screens.narratorSegment: The Development View organizes the codebase into modules, libraries, and build boundaries. It answers questions developers have when scheduling work, such as where to place a new module, how releases map to components, and which libraries are shared across features. This view can speed on-boarding because it highlights logical boundaries and ownership. For example, a monorepo may show service modules, shared libraries, and separate deployment pipelines; the Development View clarifies which teams change which modules and how versioning is handled. A trap is to confuse development modules with runtime components; keep the Development View focused on source layout, build, and dependency management. When documenting, include pointers to the README files, build scripts, and relevant ADRs that explain why the repository is structured a certain way. Good practice: update the Development View when refactoring or changing build infrastructure, and connect it to ADRs describing the reasoning for architectural changes. Development View and maintainability means shows module and repository organization to aid maintainability and team coordination.. In practical terms, organizing modules, libraries and source structure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Notation choices: UML vs C4
screens.narratorSegment: Notation matters because it shapes how clearly people understand an architecture. UML provides a wide range of diagram types — class, component, deployment, sequence — which can express detailed structural and behavioral information. This detail can be useful when teams require precise, formal diagrams, for example to model interfaces or class relationships. However, UML's comprehensiveness can be overwhelming for cross-functional stakeholders. The C4 model intentionally uses a small set of diagram levels that progressively zoom in: Context, Container, Component, and Code. C4 is especially effective for communicating across audiences because it encourages consistent abstraction layers and simpler diagrams. In practice, use C4 for high-level communication and onboarding, and reserve UML when you need formal, detailed engineering diagrams. A misconception is that one notation must replace the other; instead use them as complementary tools. For example, present a C4 container diagram to product and ops teams, and create a UML sequence diagram only if a particular runtime interaction needs precise specification. The key is selecting the right level of detail for the audience and keeping diagrams linked to ADRs and code.

screens.title: C4 model levels
screens.narratorSegment: The C4 model organizes architecture into four simple levels to help diverse audiences understand a system by zooming in progressively. The Context diagram is the highest level; it shows the system in scope, external users, and other systems it interacts with, giving a bird's-eye view. The Container diagram zooms in to show major deployable units — web apps, APIs, databases, storage — and how they communicate. The Component diagram drills into a single container to show components and their interfaces. The Code level, often generated, shows class or module details and is optional for architecture documentation. This progression is powerful because it maps naturally to different conversations: product managers want context, operators want containers and deployment, and developers may explore components or code. A common misuse is skipping levels or combining too much into one diagram; instead create separate diagrams for each level and link them together with references and ADRs. Practice: create a short text-based C4 context and container diagram for a photo-sharing app, naming actors and top-level containers to reveal responsibilities and interactions. C4 model levels means use four zoom levels so stakeholders can move from high-level context to component detail without being overwhelmed.. In practical terms, context, container, component, code — a progressive zoom. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
screens.narratorSegment: Architecture Decision Records provide a lightweight, versioned way to explain why an important architectural choice was made. An ADR typically includes a title, status, context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, date, and author. The goal is not exhaustiveness but a clear, discoverable explanation so future teams can understand historical reasoning. A concrete example: deciding to use a relational database for order processing can be captured in an ADR that explains ACID requirements, alternatives like NoSQL and managed enterprise databases, and the trade-offs. Store ADRs with the code so they evolve with the system and reference them from pull requests. A common mistake is writing ADRs after the fact with little context; the ADR is most valuable when it records the context and options considered at the time of decision. For practical drafting: state the context, list reasonable alternatives, declare the decision with supporting rationale, and enumerate positive and negative consequences. Closing question: which of your last three major decisions would benefit from a short ADR to reduce future rework? In practical terms, a concise template to record decisions, context, alternatives, and consequences. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
ADR quick template
Title: Clear, short description of the decision.
Status: Accepted, proposed, deprecated.
Context: Why this decision is under consideration.
Decision: The chosen solution and brief justification.
Alternatives: Other options considered and why they were rejected.
Consequences: Positive and negative outcomes to watch for.
Example excerpt
Title: Use PostgreSQL for primary data storage. Context: Need ACID guarantees for orders. Decision: Use PostgreSQL for its transactional guarantees and extensibility. Alternatives: MySQL, NoSQL solutions. Consequences: Better consistency, some operational complexity.
Practice

Draft an ADR for a message queue choice and store it with your repo. Link it to a related pull request.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why documenting software architecture is an essential engineering practice and how to make documentation clear, concise, and maintainable. Good architecture documentation is primarily a communication tool: it preserves the big decisions, explains the rationale, and helps teams make consistent choices as the system evolves. Poor or missing documentation creates confusion, causes repeated debates, and adds risk when people assume the reasons behind past choices. We will explore common architectural views, practical notation approaches like UML and the C4 model, and a lightweight way to record decisions using Architecture Decision Records. Throughout, the emphasis is on recording the why and the what at the right level of abstraction — not the implementation details that rapidly go out of date. You will see concrete examples and a short ADR template you can reuse. By the end you'll be able to pick the right view for your audience, create a C4-style container diagram for a small system, and write an ADR so future team members can understand why a choice was made. Think about one decision in your current project that would be clearer with an ADR.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why architectural documentation matters, choose the appropriate view for a stakeholder, and record key decisions so future teams understand past reasoning. Objective one helps you see documentation as a communication instrument that reduces repeated debates and implementation drift. Objective two asks you to name and distinguish common architectural views and say when each is appropriate, which helps you tailor artifacts to developers, operators, or product owners. Objective three introduces notation choices: you will recognize when UML diagrams provide useful detail and when the C4 model’s layered approach gives clearer explanations for different audiences. The final objective is hands-on: you will practice creating Architecture Decision Records that capture context, options, decisions and consequences, and store them with code. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a reason why it matters — clarity, maintainability, and historical context. Think of the next decision you will document using these techniques.

This second objectives slide turns the chapter goals into practice tasks you can perform during the lab. First, be able to write a short, readable C4 context diagram in plain text that identifies the system boundary and its key external actors. Second, create a container diagram that lists major deployable units and how they communicate — the lab will have you map web front-end, A P I, database, and storage. Third, select the right notation: decide when a UML deployment or sequence diagram helps operations, and when a C4 container diagram is clearer for product discussions. Fourth, draft a minimal ADR for a message-queue choice, including context, alternatives, the decision, and consequences. These tasks are intentionally small and repeatable so you can incorporate them into your team’s workflow. Practice keeping each artifact concise and readily discoverable where your team works; that’s as important as the content itself. After each practice step, ask: who benefits from this artifact and how often must it be updated?

Architectural documentation exists to communicate intent and constraints, not to replicate code or become a long, unmaintainable manual. Think of documentation as a shared vocabulary: it tells future maintainers what mattered when key choices were made and why certain trade-offs were accepted. For example, an ADR that explains choosing a particular database clarifies performance, consistency, and operational expectations; without that record, new engineers may propose incompatible changes that reintroduce problems. A common misconception is that more detail is always better. In practice, overly detailed architecture documents that mirror code become obsolete and create extra upkeep. Instead, aim for just enough information to answer stakeholder questions: the what, the why, and the consequences. Use short diagrams to show structure and brief ADRs to capture decisions. Another pitfall is keeping documentation isolated from the team’s workflow. Store diagrams and ADRs alongside code or in the team’s primary documentation site so they are discoverable and versioned. Takeaway: document the rationale and the structural overview; avoid implementation detail. A reflective question: which recent change in your project would have been faster if an ADR had existed?

Creating useful architecture documentation is a process that balances clarity, discoverability, and maintenance. Start by deciding the audience for each artifact: developers need a logical view and components; operations need deployment and process views. Next, choose the notation and level of detail: use UML where precise structural or behavioral detail is required, and prefer C4 diagrams for layered, audience-friendly descriptions. Third, place artifacts where teams already work — version control, developer portals, or the primary docs site — and link them to code and tickets. A common mistake is producing documents that live in a separate, rarely-visited wiki. Finally, set an update process: lightweight ADRs updated when decisions change, and diagrams reviewed during architecture reviews or major releases. For example, when a team migrates to containerized deployments, update the deployment view and record the decision in an ADR. This process reduces drift and keeps documentation actionable. Checkpoint: after documenting, ask whether the artifact answers a practitioner’s top three questions; if not, pare it back or reframe it for the intended role. Good documentation practices means document with a clear audience, store artifacts where teams work, and update them as part of the development lifecycle.. In practical terms, concise, discoverable, and role-focused documentation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Architectural views let you present the system from perspectives that match stakeholder concerns. The Logical View explains functional decomposition: major components, responsibilities, and interfaces — valuable for developers planning feature work. The Process View shows runtime behavior: concurrency, message flows, and sequence of operations — operations and performance engineers rely on it. The Deployment View maps components to physical or virtual infrastructure — critical for deployment, scaling, and network configuration. The Physical View, when separate, focuses on hardware and network topology. Finally, the Development View organizes modules and libraries to show how the codebase is managed and built. Each view answers a distinct set of questions: Who implements which responsibility? How do runtime parts communicate? Where do components run? When you prepare documentation, choose the view that answers the most urgent question for your audience. For example, when addressing latency problems, the Process View and Deployment View will be most useful together. A common misconception is to create a single monolithic diagram; instead create multiple concise views and link them to the relevant ADRs or artifacts so reviewers can navigate from rationale to structure.

The Logical View describes the system’s structure in terms of responsibilities and interactions. It groups related functionality into components, and it shows interfaces and relationships between those components. This view helps developers understand where features live and how modules collaborate. A concrete example: an e-commerce domain might include components such as Catalog, Cart, Order, and Payment. The Logical View shows the responsibilities of each component and the interfaces they expose, helping developers avoid coupling unrelated concerns.
